blocks.text: [II, 598] φάττα μὲν οὖν, καὶ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· τρυγὼν δὲ τοῦ θέρους· τοῦ γὰρ χειμῶνος ἀφανίζεται· [phatta men oun, kai peristera aei phainontai; trygōn de tou therous; tou gar cheimōnos aphanizetai] The wood-pigeon and the dove are always to be seen, but the turtledove only in summer. For in winter it is not seen. And in book 8, chapter 12, denying of the wood-pigeon the very thing he had affirmed here, he writes that only doves remain all year. His words are: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ καὶ αἱ φάτται, καὶ αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες, αἱ δὲ περιστεραὶ καταμένουσιν· [Apairousi de kai hai phattai, kai hai peleiades, kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones, hai de peristerai katamenousin] But the wood-pigeons, the rock-doves, the swallows and the turtledoves depart, and do not winter (here), but the doves remain. And in chapter 16 he teaches that it is above all characteristic of the turtledove to hide in winter. Φωλεῖ γὰρ [Phōlei gar], he says, καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος. καὶ ἥ γε τρυγὼν ὁμολογουμένως μάλιστα πάντων. οὐδεὶς γὰρ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, λέγεται τρυγόνα ἰδεῖν οὐδαμοῦ χειμῶνος· [kai pelargos, kai kottyphos, kai trygōn, kai korydos. kai hē ge trygōn homologoumenōs malista pantōn. oudeis gar, hōs eipein, legetai trygona idein oudamou cheimōnos] For the stork also hides, and the blackbird, and the turtledove, and the lark. But of the turtledove this is agreed most of all: for no one, I might almost say, is reported to have seen a turtledove anywhere in winter. Varro too, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another season turtledoves and quails in enormous numbers. And Cicero, De Finib. book 2: Turtledoves delight in running and in travel. And Gregory of Nyssa on the Song, Homily 5: Ἐν γὰρ τῇ χειμῶνι φεύγει ἡ ἀηδὼν, ναρκᾷ ἡ χελιδὼν, ἀποξενοῦται τῆς καλίας ἡ τρυγών· [En gar tē cheimōni pheugei hē aēdōn, narka hē chelidōn, apoxenoutai tēs kalias hē trygōn] For in winter the nightingale flees, the swallow grows torpid, the turtledove goes abroad from its nest. There are some, however, who think that the turtledove does not so much go away as hide. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: More truly, the turtledove hides and loses its feathers. Others wrongly read vere [in spring]. For the turtledove does not hide in spring, but in winter. Indeed Aristotle himself, in chapter 12 cited above, does not deny that some turtledoves remain ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις [en euēliois chōriois].

In Cant. I, 10. it is said to the bride in the Greek version, Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos?] and in the Vulgate, How beautiful are your cheeks become, like the turtledove's! On this passage the Greek doctors, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Philo of Carpasia, Theodoret, and the Latin ones, Justus of Urgel, Gregory the Great, Bede, Aponius, Bernard, and other men of great name, have much to say about the chastity of the turtledove and about the seat of modesty in the cheeks. But all of it is beside the point, if I may say so with their leave. For the passage is not about the turtledove there: since it has no σιαγόνες [siagones], that is, cheeks or jaws, who would believe that the bride's cheeks are compared with the cheeks of a turtledove? Ἡ δὲ ὄρνις [Hē de ornis] (says the Philosopher, De partib. animal. book 2, ch. 16)

[II, 599] ἀντὶ σιαγόνων ἔχει τὸ καλούμενον ῥύγχος [anti siagonōn echei to kaloumenon rhynchos], in place of jaws it has what they call a beak. In vain would you object that Ovid, at the death of his parrot, invites the other birds to tear their cheeks, in Amores book 2, Elegy 6:
Go, pious birds, and beat your breasts with your wings, and mark your tender cheeks with rigid claw.

For he is applying to birds ποιητικῶς [poiētikōs], and πρωσοποποιητικῶς [prōsopopoiētikōs], things that are proper to human beings in mourning. [col. 57] Accordingly the same poet, Tristia book 3, Elegy 3:
Yet forbear to tear your cheeks, and do not rend your hair.
Do not wound my shade, but spare your loosened hair, and spare, Delia, your tender cheeks,
